title: Zhui invested in Unitree but missed the follow-on: patient capital gets stuck by fund cycles too
dek: Vertex was the sole institutional investor in Unitree's Pre-A+ round in 2020, but in the 2023 round it couldn't follow on because its own USD fund was expiring and it was raising a new fund. Doubling down tests not just vision but the match between fund and project timing.
why: A person who has done hard-tech VC for 17 years within Singapore's sovereign capital system lays out the betting logic for chips, robotics and low-altitude economy, and candidly reviews why he missed ByteDance and the Unitree follow-on.
who: For founders and investors focused on hard tech, robotics and the fundraising-investment-management-exit of USD funds, especially those who want to know how a sovereign-backed VC makes independent judgments and reviews missed follow-ons.
skip: 27:35 to 33:28 covers Singapore clan associations, the Zhongyuan Festival and Chinese cohesion, which is weakly related to investment judgment.

points.h: They started investing when chips were cheaper than potato chips
points.body: Vertex invested in semiconductors as early as 2011, and in 2012 in a new-materials company making solid-state batteries. At the time almost no domestic VC looked at these, because the internet was at its peak. Zheng Juncong told a joke: chips are called chips, and everyone thought a chip was cheaper than a potato chip, so nobody invested, because chips were imported and sold for only one US dollar each. He judged that chips have extremely high technical content, from millions of lines of code to billions of lines of code, and all electronic products, cars and the cloud need them. The pitch for investing in chips also changed with the times: first it was domestic production being tax-free, then iterating around the mobile phone supply chain, and now it's about being strangled plus next-generation applications like optical computing.

points.h: IC can pass by half, and there's a golden share
points.body: Vertex's investment committee doesn't need a unanimous vote; a majority suffices, and they even convene ad hoc on weekends when a project needs to go to IC. More unusually, there's a golden share: a partner has one chance a year to force investment in a company even if the IC rejects it. Votes are secret; you don't know whether a partner voted yes or no, because they don't want people doing favors for each other and abandoning independent judgment. Voting choices are also tied to project outcomes long-term: if a project fails but you voted yes, it's traced back into your score, and when carry is distributed they pull it out to look at. This mechanism is designed to force independent judgment, not personal favors.

points.h: They don't chase trends because founders of fought-over projects get cocky
points.body: Vertex explicitly does not invest in projects that are especially sought after in the market. Zheng Juncong gives two reasons: first, everyone fighting drives up the valuation; second, when a founder is fought over, he focuses on valuation and feels investors are all fawning over him, so he won't settle down to build the company, and the success rate is actually lower. They value founders who do solid technology, have patience, want to create value, and don't rely on hype. They have zero tolerance for financial fraud, because Singapore cares a lot about integrity and authenticity, and once fraud is discovered they will definitely exit. This style also explains why they haven't invested in many money-burning internet companies.

points.h: Given another chance on large models, still no, because it's like the internet
points.body: Over the past four years China's investment hotspot has undoubtedly been AI large models, and Vertex didn't make a move in the first three or four years, which is very unusual among first-tier funds. Zheng Juncong's reasoning: large-model startups in China have no advantage; the advantage will come from customers, data and application scenarios, and it requires being big enough and able to burn a lot of money; it's essentially an internet playbook, and the business model is still unclear. The two biggest internal voices were "this will definitely take off, China will definitely have large models" and "the model risk is high, it may keep burning money like the internet, and existing large internet companies have a higher probability of success." He admits this discourages young investors who want to participate, but they held back because they firmly believe hard tech is the advantage.

points.h: Singapore certification: swap chips and software, then export
points.body: Zheng Juncong believes Singapore can help Chinese entrepreneurs solve two things: product internationalization and product security. Products made from China's manufacturing, design and innovation capabilities are wanted worldwide, but geopolitics gets in the way, with politicians obstructing on grounds that "Chinese products are unsafe, robots might carry things and hit people on the street." Singapore, as a neutral, transparent and reputable country, can achieve "Citified by Singapore"—chips certified here, or swapped for chips and software here, then exported from here, allowing products to enter other countries. He also criticizes "Singapore Washing": companies that move here just to slap on a label without actual operations and R&D—the term he least wants to hear.

points.h: Boston Dynamics costs over $100k, Wang Xingxing sells for over $10k
points.body: In 2019 Zheng Juncong went to Boston for a board meeting and visited Boston Dynamics. He wanted to buy a robot dog, but they said it wasn't for sale; the cost was about over $100,000. Back in China, he judged that China is strong in hardware and someone must be doing it, so he had his team search all Chinese robotics teams and found Wang Xingxing. At the time the robot dog was already very agile, able to stand up and bow. He asked if it was controlled by AI; Wang Xingxing said no, it used his own algorithm. Asked about cost, Wang Xingxing didn't mention cost, only said it currently sells for about over $10,000. The same dog, with others' cost at over $100,000, he sells for over $10,000. Zheng Juncong judged there was commercialization potential; cost is a very important element in technological innovation.

points.h: Missed Unitree follow-on: fund expired, not enough bullets
points.body: Vertex was the sole institutional investor in Unitree's Pre-A+ round in 2020, but the follow-on only came in September 2024, when Unitree had already produced the G1 bipedal robot and its valuation had soared. Why didn't they follow on earlier? Zheng Juncong reviews: when they invested, they saw a market of several billion, not that bipedal robots could be made; in the 2023 round, Matrix Partners and Shunwei came in, and they also wanted to invest, but their USD fund was exactly at the end of its term and they were raising a new fund, so they didn't have enough bullets to add to the position, and they missed that round. He calls it a huge regret, and says it made them reflect; now the new fund requires starting to raise new capital once 65% is invested, reserving 20% to 30% for follow-ons.

points.h: Wang Xingxing raised slowly, but that forged mass-production consistency
points.body: Zheng Juncong believes Wang Xingxing doesn't need to be better at fundraising; the current fundraising pace is actually the best. If back then he had been good at fundraising and raised a lot in the next round, the playbook might have been different—flashy, more money-burning, no discipline in running the company, not nitpicking cost details, and the models produced might not be profitable. After AI arrived, many companies want to copy Unitree, thinking the barrier isn't high, it's just algorithms, and they can catch up quickly with AI. Zheng Juncong says everyone can get algorithms to about the same level, but the real gap is mass production and consistency, which is built up from all past investment and time, and no second company in the market has his mass-production consistency.

points.h: A crude way to judge bubbles: look at who is starting companies
points.body: Asked whether China's embodied intelligence has a bubble, Zheng Juncong says no, because the market is still expanding and in its creation phase. He gives a rough indicator for judging bubbles: when the entrepreneurs you attract are not real entrepreneurs, but people from big companies without entrepreneurial spirit who see others succeed and raise money and jump out saying they want to start a company too—that's the point when a bubble appears. Now he sees entrepreneurs who are "I've done this and that," very strong and capable people. He quotes Lee Kuan Yew: the market needs bubbles, like beer without foam isn't tasty, but too much foam isn't good either; it must be kept at an appropriate proportion.

terms.def: Vertex's investment committee mechanism: a partner can, once a year, force investment in a project rejected by the IC.
Distributions to Paid-In Capital: cash actually returned to LPs divided by invested principal, the hardest metric sovereign funds use to assess GPs.
Refers to Chinese companies that only slap a Singapore headquarters label on themselves without actual operations and R&D.
Electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft, the core category of the low-altitude economy, replacing a helicopter's single engine with multiple electric rotors.
Using AI to research new materials, chemical structures and other problems humans cannot calculate.
